title: Consequentialism
description: Surveys the family of views holding that an act's rightness depends solely on its consequences, tracing the distinctions consequentialists draw between actual, foreseen, and rule-based versions of the theory.
author: Walter Sinnott-Armstrong

title: Kant's Moral Philosophy
description: Walks through Kant's Categorical Imperative and the idea that moral duty is grounded in rational autonomy rather than in consequences or desires.
author: Robert Johnson & Adam Cureton

title: Virtue Ethics
description: Traces virtue ethics from Aristotle's concept of eudaimonia through its 20th-century revival as an alternative to consequentialism and deontology.
author: Rosalind Hursthouse & Glen Pettigrove

title: Contemporary Approaches to the Social Contract
description: Explains how modern thinkers from Rawls to Gauthier reframed the classical social contract as an argument from rational agreement rather than historical consent.
author: Fred D'Agostino, Gerald Gaus & John Thrasher

title: John Rawls
description: Covers Rawls's life and the core architecture of justice as fairness, including the original position and the two principles of justice.
author: Samuel Freeman

title: War
description: Lays out just war theory's attempt to find a middle path between pacifism and realism, covering jus ad bellum and jus in bello criteria.
author: SEP contributors

title: The Problem of Evil
description: Sets out the logical and evidential versions of the problem of evil and the main theistic responses, including theodicies and skeptical theism.
author: Michael Tooley

title: Pascal's Wager
description: Reconstructs Pascal's decision-theoretic argument for believing in God and reviews the classic objections to betting on faith.
author: Paul Bartha

title: Ontological Arguments
description: Traces the ontological argument from Anselm's original a priori proof of God's existence through Kant's and later Gödel's and Plantinga's responses.
author: Kenneth Himma & Graham Oppy

title: Theological Voluntarism
description: Examines divine command theory's central claim that moral obligation is constituted by God's will, and its main historical and contemporary variants.
author: Michael J. Murray & Kyle Rupp

title: Social Contract Theory
description: Introduces how Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau each used the idea of an agreement among free persons to justify political authority, plus its Rawlsian revival.
author: IEP contributors

title: Philosophy of Religion
description: A broad overview of the field's core questions — religious language, arguments for God, the problem of evil, and religious diversity — aimed at newcomers.
author: IEP contributors

title: John Rawls
description: Summarizes how A Theory of Justice revived social contract thinking to defend an egalitarian-liberal account of justice.
author: IEP contributors

title: Utilitarianism
description: Mill's 1861 defense of the greatest-happiness principle, including his attempt to distinguish higher and lower pleasures against charges that utilitarianism is a "pig philosophy."
author: John Stuart Mill

title: The Nicomachean Ethics
description: Aristotle's foundational treatise arguing that the good life consists in virtuous activity guided by practical wisdom rather than pleasure or duty alone.
author: Aristotle (trans. W.D. Ross)

title: Leviathan
description: Hobbes's 1651 argument that only an absolute sovereign, authorized by mutual covenant, can rescue people from the violent "state of nature."
author: Thomas Hobbes

title: Second Treatise of Government
description: Locke's case for government by consent, natural rights to life, liberty, and property, and the right of the people to resist a government that violates the trust.
author: John Locke

title: The Social Contract & Discourses
description: Rousseau's account of legitimate political authority as an expression of the "general will," opening with his famous line that "man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains."
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau

title: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
description: A three-way debate between Demea, Cleanthes, and Philo that stress-tests the design argument and other attempts to infer God's nature from the natural world.
author: David Hume

title: Groundwork for the Metaphysic of Morals
description: A modernized-English edition of Kant's 1785 text deriving the Categorical Imperative as the supreme principle of morality from reason alone.
author: Immanuel Kant (ed. Jonathan Bennett)

title: Introduction to Political Philosophy
description: A full 24-lecture Yale course moving from Plato and Aristotle's polis through Machiavelli, Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau to Tocqueville on democracy.
author: Steven B. Smith

title: The Rawlsian Social Contract
description: A single lecture unpacking Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance as a Kantian-style thought experiment for choosing principles of justice.
author: Ian Shapiro

title: Justice
description: A full course syllabus, lecture notes, and assignments comparing utilitarianism, libertarianism, and egalitarian liberalism as rival theories of a just society.
author: Lucas Stanczyk

title: Justice: What's The Right Thing To Do? — The Moral Side of Murder
description: The opening lecture of Sandel's famous course, using the trolley problem and an 1884 shipwreck-cannibalism case to introduce students to utilitarian reasoning and its limits.
author: Michael J. Sandel

title: Utilitarianism
description: A brief animated explainer defining utilitarianism as the view that the morally right act maximizes overall well-being.
author: Ethics Unwrapped / UT Austin

title: Virtue Ethics
description: A short animated explainer introducing virtue ethics as a character-centered alternative to rule- and consequence-based moral theories.
author: Ethics Unwrapped / UT Austin

title: Ethics and God: Divine Command Theory and the Euthyphro Dilemma
description: A concise essay laying out divine command theory and Plato's Euthyphro dilemma — is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it's good?
author: Nathan Nobis

title: The Problem of Evil: Is Suffering Evidence That There Is Not a God?
description: A brief essay explaining why suffering is taken as evidence against theism and surveying replies like the free-will defense and skeptical theism.
author: Thomas Metcalf

title: Consequentialism and Utilitarianism
description: A short introduction distinguishing consequentialism generally from its best-known form, utilitarianism, and the "greatest happiness" standard.
author: Shane Gronholz

title: Stephen Law on the Problem of Evil
description: Philosopher Stephen Law presents his "evil god challenge," arguing it is just as hard to refute a wholly evil god as a wholly good one.
author: Stephen Law, interviewed by Nigel Warburton & David Edmonds

title: Jonathan Wolff on John Rawls' A Theory of Justice
description: Political philosopher Jonathan Wolff explains the original position and veil of ignorance and discusses key objections to Rawls's theory.
author: Jonathan Wolff, interviewed by Nigel Warburton & David Edmonds

title: The Ox Heard Round the World: Thomas Aquinas
description: An introduction to Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotle and Christian theology, including his Five Ways arguments for God's existence.
author: Peter Adamson
sourceName: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps

title: John Rawls: His Life and Theory of Justice
description: A critical review engaging Pogge's biography-plus-exposition of Rawls, focusing on disputes over whether the original position is too "recipient-oriented."
author: Arthur Kuflik

title: Ethics: A Free Online Course
description: Points to a 32-lecture video course spanning egoism and Plato's contractarians through Aristotle, Aquinas, Kant, and utilitarianism.
author: Gregory Sadler

title: The Republic
description: Plato's dialogue constructing an ideal city to answer the question of what justice is and why it is worth pursuing for its own sake.
author: Plato (trans. Benjamin Jowett)

title: Just War Theory: Revisionists vs. Traditionalists
description: A scholarly survey of the split between Walzer's traditionalist just war theory and the "revisionist" school that judges combatants by individual moral responsibility.
author: Seth Lazar

title: Kant: Categorical Imperative
description: A curated bibliography page collecting scholarly articles on Kant's Categorical Imperative, useful as a jumping-off point for further reading.
author: PhilPapers editors

title: The Problem of Evil for Atheists
description: An open-access book arguing that the problem of evil is not just a theist's problem — it also poses a challenge for atheists, pantheists, and other non-theistic worldviews.
author: Yujin Nagasawa

title: Personal Identity
description: Surveys the different questions bundled under "personal identity" — what makes someone the same person over time — and compares psychological, biological, and narrative answers.
author: Eric T. Olson

title: Identity Over Time
description: Works through classic puzzles of persistence, including the Ship of Theseus, and the competing three-dimensionalist and four-dimensionalist replies to them.
author: André Gallois

title: Free Will
description: Maps the free will debate — libertarianism, hard determinism, and compatibilism — and the arguments each side uses against the others.
author: Timothy O'Connor & Christopher Evan Franklin

title: The Analysis of Knowledge
description: Traces the "justified true belief" account of knowledge, Gettier's famous counterexamples to it, and the main attempts to patch or replace the analysis.
author: Jonathan Jenkins Ichikawa & Matthias Steup

title: The Problem of Induction
description: Lays out Hume's argument that inductive reasoning can't be rationally justified without circularity, plus later attempts to answer him.
author: Leah Henderson

title: The Chinese Room Argument
description: Explains Searle's thought experiment against machine understanding and catalogs the major replies (systems, robot, brain simulator, and others).
author: David Cole

title: Dualism
description: Covers substance and property dualism as responses to the mind-body problem, along with the standard objections to each.
author: Howard Robinson & Ralph Weir

title: Qualia: The Knowledge Argument
description: Unpacks Frank Jackson's "Mary's Room" thought experiment about a color scientist who has never seen color, and what it's supposed to show about physicalism.
author: Martine Nida-Rümelin & Donnchadh O Conaill

title: Aristotle: Logic
description: Walks through Aristotle's Organon and the categorical syllogism, showing how he tied argument validity to logical form rather than content.
author: IEP contributors

title: Functionalism
description: Introduces the view that mental states are defined by their causal role rather than their physical makeup, and why that helps with multiple realizability.
author: Thomas Polger

title: Validity and Soundness
description: A short, worked-example guide to the difference between a valid argument and a sound one.
author: IEP contributors

title: Deductive and Inductive Arguments
description: Compares deductive certainty with inductive probability using everyday example arguments.
author: IEP contributors

title: Epistemology
description: A broad-survey entry point into theory-of-knowledge questions: sources of knowledge, justification, and skepticism.
author: IEP contributors

title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
description: Hume's own accessible restatement of his empiricist epistemology, including his argument against justifying induction.
author: David Hume

title: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
description: Mill's 1843 treatise laying out his "methods" of inductive inference and a full account of logic as applied to scientific reasoning.
author: John Stuart Mill

title: Symbolic Logic
description: Carroll's playful, puzzle-driven introduction to categorical syllogisms and diagrammatic logic.
author: Lewis Carroll

title: Meditations on First Philosophy
description: A modernized-English edition of Descartes' six Meditations, tracking his method of doubt through to the cogito and the mind-body distinction.
author: René Descartes (Jonathan Bennett rendering)

title: Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous
description: Berkeley's dialogue defending idealism — the claim that to be is to be perceived — against a materialist interlocutor.
author: George Berkeley (Jonathan Bennett rendering)

title: Logic I
description: A full undergraduate course covering truth tables, formal derivations, and the soundness/completeness of propositional and predicate logic.
author: Ephraim Glick

title: Theory of Knowledge
description: A semester-long epistemology course built around skeptical arguments (brain-in-a-vat, evil demon) and the responses to them.
author: Declan Smithies

title: Death
description: Roughly a third of this full lecture course is devoted to dualism vs. physicalism and competing theories of personal identity, before turning to the nature of death itself.
author: Shelly Kagan

title: The Gettier Problem and the Definition of Knowledge
description: A compact walkthrough of Gettier's counterexamples to "knowledge = justified true belief" and the fourth-condition fixes philosophers have proposed.
author: Andrew Chapman

title: The Mind-Body Problem: What Are Minds?
description: Introduces dualism, identity theory, and functionalism as three competing answers to what minds fundamentally are.
author: Jacob Berger

title: Free Will and Free Choice
description: A short overview of libertarianism, hard determinism, and compatibilism as answers to whether free will is compatible with a determined universe.
author: Jonah Nagashima

title: The Gettier Problem No Longer a Problem
description: A magazine-style essay arguing that Gettier's original cases contain hidden flaws, offering a contrarian angle for classroom debate on the knowledge-analysis literature.
author: Lukasz Lozanski

title: Gary Hatfield on Descartes' Meditations
description: A conversation with a leading Descartes scholar on the structure and aims of the Meditations, including the doubt-based method and the mind-body split.
author: Peter Adamson, with guest Gary Hatfield
sourceName: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps

title: Christopher Shields on Personal Identity
description: Shields discusses Locke's memory theory and rival accounts of what makes someone the same person across time.
author: Christopher Shields

title: Ned Block on Consciousness
description: Block distinguishes phenomenal consciousness from cognitive access to it, using attention experiments and clinical cases as evidence.
author: Ned Block

title: The Mind-Body Problem and Metaphysics
description: A critical review of a recent book defending substance dualism via the conceivability argument, useful as a model of how professional philosophers evaluate a metaphysical thesis.
author: Alin Cucu (reviewing Ralph Stefan Weir)

title: Organon and Other Logical Works
description: The full set of Aristotle's logical treatises — Categories, On Interpretation, Prior and Posterior Analytics, Topics, Sophistical Refutations — in one public-domain volume.
author: Aristotle (trans. W. D. Ross et al.)

title: Critique of Pure Reason
description: Kant's attempt to fix the limits of what reason can know, reconciling rationalist and empiricist starting points through transcendental idealism.
author: Immanuel Kant

title: Symbolic Logic: A Free Online Course
description: A 15-lecture video course covering truth tables, truth trees, and formal derivation in propositional and first-order logic.
author: John Sanders

title: Experimental Metaphysics
description: An edited collection asking whether empirical, cognitive-science methods can inform classic metaphysical questions about free will, causation, and objects.
author: David Rose (ed.)

title: Introduction to Philosophy: Epistemology
description: An open-license textbook chapter set covering justification, skepticism, the value of knowledge, and social epistemology, written for first-year students.
author: Brian C. Barnett (ed.)

title: Introduction to Philosophy: Logic
description: An open-license introductory logic textbook covering argument evaluation, formal logic basics, and informal fallacies.
author: Benjamin Martin et al. (eds.)

title: Beauty
description: A survey of philosophical theories of beauty, from classical objectivist accounts to modern subjectivist and relational views, tracing how the concept has been treated across the history of aesthetics.
author: Crispin Sartwell

title: Aesthetic Experience
description: Examines what distinguishes an aesthetic experience from ordinary perception, and reviews competing theories about its role in defining art and artistic value.
author: Antonia Peacocke

title: Aesthetics
description: A broad introduction to aesthetics as the philosophical study of beauty and art, covering major historical positions from the eighteenth century to the present.
author: Barry Hartley Slater

title: The Poetics
description: Aristotle's foundational treatise on tragedy, epic poetry, and artistic imitation (mimesis), including his influential account of catharsis and dramatic structure.
author: Aristotle (trans. S. H. Butcher)

title: Critique of Judgement
description: Kant's third critique, developing his theory of aesthetic judgment, the beautiful, and the sublime, and arguing that judgments of taste claim universal validity without relying on determinate concepts.
author: Immanuel Kant (trans. J. H. Bernard)

title: Of the Standard of Taste
description: Hume's 1757 essay arguing that although taste varies widely, some critical judgments about art are better grounded than others, based on the responses of experienced and unbiased critics.
author: David Hume (Jonathan Bennett rendering)

title: Studies in Poetry: What's the Use of Beauty?
description: A full MIT course syllabus pairing poems with foundational aesthetic theory from Plato and Kant to twentieth-century critics, exploring whether recognizing beauty can shape moral character.
author: Noel Jackson / MIT

title: Definitions of Art: What is Art?
description: A short survey of competing definitions of art — representational, expressionist, formalist, and institutional theories — and the objections each faces.
author: Brock Rough

title: Elisabeth Schellekens Dammann on Disagreement About Taste
description: A philosopher of aesthetics discusses why people disagree about matters of taste and whether such disagreements can ever really be resolved.
author: Elisabeth Schellekens Dammann, interviewed by Nigel Warburton

title: Aesthetics and Nature
description: A scholarly review of a book on the aesthetic appreciation of the natural environment and its role in arguments for wilderness preservation.
author: Mara Miller (reviewing Glenn Parsons)

title: Existentialism
description: A comprehensive overview of existentialism, tracing its central commitments — concrete existence, freedom, and authenticity — through Kierkegaard, Heidegger, Sartre, and others.
author: Kevin Aho

title: Camus, Albert
description: An overview of Albert Camus's life and philosophy, focusing on his concept of the absurd and his famously ambivalent relationship to the existentialist label.
author: David Simpson

title: Kierkegaard, Søren
description: Introduces Kierkegaard's pseudonymous writings and key concepts such as anxiety, despair, and the leap of faith that shaped later existentialist thought.
author: William McDonald

title: Sartre, Jean Paul: Existentialism
description: Explains Sartre's core existentialist claims, including "existence precedes essence," radical freedom, and bad faith.
author: Christian J. Onof

title: Mary Warnock on Sartre's Existentialism
description: Philosopher Mary Warnock discusses Sartre's claim that human beings are radically free and responsible for creating their own values through their choices.
author: Mary Warnock, interviewed by Nigel Warburton

title: An Animated Introduction to Albert Camus' Existentialism
description: A short animated lesson summarizing Camus's philosophy of the absurd and his argument that life can be meaningful even without a cosmic purpose.
author: TED-Ed (narrated by Nina Medvinskaya)

title: Søren Kierkegaard: A Free Online Course
description: A set of free video lectures giving a detailed introduction to Kierkegaard's life, authorship, and place at the origin of existentialist philosophy.
author: Jon B. Stewart

title: Camus on the Absurd: The Myth of Sisyphus
description: Explains Camus's Myth of Sisyphus and his central question of whether life is worth living once its lack of inherent meaning is confronted honestly.
author: Erik Van Aken

title: The Cambridge Companion to Existentialism
description: A scholarly review of a companion volume introducing the major figures and central concepts of existentialism to students encountering the movement for the first time.
author: Michael R. Kelly (reviewing Steven Crowell, ed.)

title: Daoism
description: An overview of Daoism as a philosophical tradition, covering the Daodejing and Zhuangzi and central concepts such as the Dao, wu-wei, and naturalness.
author: Chad Hansen

title: Zhuangzi
description: A detailed treatment of Zhuangzi's ideas about perspective, skepticism, spontaneity, and the relativity of human judgments and values.
author: Chad Hansen

title: Confucius
description: An introduction to Confucius's life and ethical-political thought, including his views on ritual propriety, humaneness (ren), and the cultivation of virtue.
author: Jeff Richey

title: Nagarjuna
description: Explains the Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka teachings on emptiness (sunyata) and his critique of essentialist metaphysics.
author: Douglas Berger

title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
description: James Legge's classic English translation of the Daodejing, the foundational text of Daoism traditionally attributed to Laozi.
author: Laozi (trans. James Legge)

title: The Analects of Confucius
description: A public-domain translation of the Analects, the collected sayings of Confucius and his disciples on ethics, ritual, and governance.
author: Confucius (trans. James Legge)

title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses
description: F. Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, a core collection of verses attributed to the Buddha on ethical conduct and the path to liberation from suffering.
author: attributed to the Buddha (trans. F. Max Müller)

title: No Four Ways About It: Nāgārjuna's Tetralemma
description: A podcast episode unpacking Nagarjuna's four-cornered logic (the tetralemma) and its use in arguing that phenomena lack independent existence.
author: Peter Adamson, with Jonardon Ganeri
sourceName: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps

title: Suffering and Smiling: the Buddha
description: A podcast episode introducing the Buddha's life and core teachings, including the Four Noble Truths and the doctrine of no-self.
author: Peter Adamson, with Jonardon Ganeri
sourceName: History of Philosophy Without Any Gaps

title: The Complete Works of Chuang Tzu
description: Burton Watson's widely used English translation of the Zhuangzi, one of the two foundational texts of philosophical Daoism, freely readable online.
author: Zhuangzi (trans. Burton Watson)

title: Nothingness in Asian Philosophy
description: An open-access essay collection comparing how Hindu, Buddhist, Daoist, and Neo-Confucian traditions have conceptualized "nothingness" as a philosophical category.
author: JeeLoo Liu and Douglas L. Berger (eds.)
